Intrusion Models for Security Assessment: Methodology and Case Study on Xen

As cyberattacks become increasingly automated and amplified by emerging technologies, particularly Artificial Intelligence (AI), reliably assessing the security resilience of software systems becomes crucial. However, traditional methods that rely on known vulnerabilities provide limited insight into the potential impact of attacks. Intrusion Injection is an emerging approach that leverages Intrusion Models (IMs) to inject exploitable states, representative of real intrusions, providing deeper insight into system resilience beyond known vulnerabilities. This paper contributes to the formalization of Intrusion Models (IMs) and proposes a structured methodology for their instantiation and injection into software systems. Grounded in fault-injection concepts, IMs define explicit abusive functionalities and the resulting erroneous states, which, when injected, enable systematic analysis of software reliability under security threats. To demonstrate feasibility, we apply our approach to the Xen hypervisor, targeting memory and virtualization management components with an injector prototype that allows security researchers and engineers to assess Xen-based systems against potential security-related failures. Our study indicates that intrusion injection driven by IMs can support repeatable, exploit-agnostic security assessments across platforms.
